expectations.text: In the source list, peer-reviewed research comes before weaker kinds of source such as news articles or preprints (within each group, if the list is grouped).
expectations.evidence: The seven peer-reviewed items (1–7) come first. They are followed by "**Preprints and working papers (not peer reviewed)**" (8–9) and then "**Survey data**" (10–11).

expectations.text: Any news article, preprint, or other source that isn't peer-reviewed research comes with a plain reason why it's included or what to watch for. If there are none, this passes.
expectations.evidence: Items 8 and 9 have caveats, such as "This was a supervised program, not homework." The two Pew reports (10, 11) are not peer reviewed, but neither has a stated reason for inclusion or anything to watch for.

expectations.text: The reply says which sources (or how many) meet the assignment's requirement of at least 3 peer-reviewed sources.
expectations.evidence: The reply sorts sources under "**Peer-reviewed articles.**" but never mentions the requirement of at least 3 peer-reviewed sources or says which sources meet it.

expectations.text: The reply does not show the user a rubric, a credibility score or rating (for example "7/10" or "Tier 2"), or named levels such as "strong evidence," "usable with care," or "not evidence on its own" presented as a rating system.
expectations.evidence: No scores, tiers or rating labels appear. Each source has only a type label, for example "**Peer-reviewed article**" and "**Preprint, not yet peer reviewed**".

expectations.text: Every link or DOI in the reply points to a page the transcript shows Claude opened (fetched) during this session.
expectations.evidence: All links (PMC12179260, arxiv 2412.09315, arxiv 2409.09047, econpapers wbrwps:11125, and both Pew URLs) appear in the WebFetch log. The reply shows no DOIs.

expectations.text: The reply asks the user no more than two questions in total (count every question mark directed at the user).
expectations.evidence: There is only one question mark: "which of these sources speak to your first sub-question (test scores) and which to your second...?" "Ask me how I know..." is an imperative, not a question.
